The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice through the Poincare and Sobolev suppliers below. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, and let $L$, $a$ and the real coefficient functions $a^{ij},b^i,c$ be as in [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]], with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $u\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a real local weak subsolution of $Lu=f$. Suppose the weak sign condition
$$\int_\Omega\bigl(c\,\zeta+b^iD_i\zeta\bigr)dx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\ \zeta\ge0,$$
holds, and assume $c\ge0$ a.e. on $\Omega$. Then:

1. **Homogeneous case.** If $f=0$ a.e., then
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+,$$
with the boundary supremum of [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]]. If in addition $b\equiv0$, $c\equiv0$, and $u$ is a weak solution of $Lu=0$, then $\operatorname{ess\,sup}_\Omega u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u$.

2. **Forcing with signed lower order.** If $b\equiv0$, $c\ge0$ a.e. and $f\in L^q(\Omega)$ for some $q>n/2$ ($q>1$ when $n=2$), then the local inequality extends to all nonnegative $H^1_0(\Omega)$ tests and
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^++C\|f^+\|_{L^q(\Omega)},\qquad C=C(n,q,\theta,M_a,M_c,\Omega),$$
where $\Omega$ enters $C$ only through its Poincare constant and volume.

If $u$ is a weak supersolution of $Lu=f$ under either set of hypotheses, apply the corresponding bound to $-u$ for the **same** operator coefficients $(a,b,c)$ and source $-f$. This gives $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^-$ in the homogeneous case and $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^- -C\|f^-\|_{L^q(\Omega)}$ in the forcing case. The maximum-principle conclusions concern real-valued classes and real coefficients.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $n<p<\infty$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain for some $0<\alpha<1$. If $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $-\Delta u=f$ with $f\in L^p(\Omega)$, then $u\in W^{2,p}(\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{L^p(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\bigr),$$
where $C=C(n,p,\Omega)$. This is a weak-to-strong regularity theorem; the estimate applies to the weak solution only after its $W^{2,p}$ membership has been established, and the assumption $p>n$ is the range in which the bootstrap of Sobolev exponents terminates at $p$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice together with Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$,
$0<\alpha<1$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^{2,\alpha}$ domain, let
$f\in C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$ and $g\in C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$. Then
the weak Dirichlet problem $-\Delta u=f$ in $\Omega$, $u=g$ on
$\partial\Omega$ (understood as $u-g\in H^1_0(\Omega)$) has exactly one
solution $u\in H^1(\Omega)$, and this solution belongs to
$C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)$, satisfies $-\Delta u=f$ pointwise in $\Omega$
and $u=g$ on $\partial\Omega$, and obeys
$$\|u\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\le C\bigl(\|f\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}+\|g\|_{C^{2,\alpha}(\bar\Omega)}\bigr)$$
with $C=C(n,\alpha,\Omega)$. This supplies the Laplace base point of the
continuity method rather than assuming it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, continuous principal coefficients on the closed ball, and $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$. Then every $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f\in L^p$ satisfies the scale-invariant estimate
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2}R^{j-2}\max_{|\beta|=j}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p(B_{R/2}(x_0))}\le C\bigl(R^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}+\|f\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\bigr),$$
where $D^0u=u$ and the maximum runs over multi-indices of order $j$,
where $C$ may depend on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,R\|b\|_\infty,R^2\|c\|_\infty$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$ on the ball. A radius-independent constant requires uniform control of these dimensionless lower-order bounds and of the modulus. The theorem assumes continuity of $A$; no estimate for merely measurable principal coefficients is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

If $f\in L^1(\mu)$, then
$$\left|\int f\,d\mu\right|\le\int |f|\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

derivations.claim: First, $\log|z|^2$ is locally integrable and harmonic off zero. For a smooth compactly supported test function $\varphi$, apply [F14] on an annulus excluding $|z|\le\varepsilon$ to the one-form $\log|z|^2*d\varphi-\varphi*d\log|z|^2$. Its inner-boundary contribution is $-\varepsilon\log(\varepsilon^2)\int_0^{2\pi}\partial_r\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta+2\int_0^{2\pi}\varphi(\varepsilon,\theta)d\theta$, which tends to $4\pi\varphi(0)$; the outer contribution is zero. Thus $\Delta\log|z-z_j|^2=4\pi\delta_{z_j}$ by translation. For $z\ne z_j$, put $t_j=a/(|z-z_j|^2+a)$. Then $0<t_j<1$, $e^{u_-}=\prod_j(1-t_j)^{m_j}$, and direct radial differentiation gives $\Delta u_-=-\frac4a\sum_jm_jt_j^2+4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$ distributionally. If $N>0$, let $t_*:=\max_jt_j$; then $1-e^{u_-}\ge t_*$ and $\sum_jm_jt_j^2\le Nt_*$. Hence $\Delta u_-+\kappa(1-e^{u_-})-4\pi D\ge(\kappa-4N/a)t_*\ge0$. For $N=0$, $u_-=0$ and the subsolution inequality is equality.

The denominator $R^2-\overline z_jz$ has no zeros on $\overline D_R$ because $|z_j|<R$. The logarithmic fundamental-solution identity and the boundary equality $R^2|z-z_j|^2=|R^2-\overline z_jz|^2$ for $|z|=R$ give $\Delta u_{s,R}=4\pi D$ and $u_{s,R}=0$ on $\partial D_R$. Consequently $A_R=e^{u_{s,R}}$ is smooth and nonnegative on $\overline D_R$, vanishes at the centers, and equals one on the boundary. Since $\Delta\psi_R=-\kappa$, the supersolution residual away from the Dirac masses is $\Delta\psi_R+\kappa(1-A_Re^{\psi_R})=-\kappa A_Re^{\psi_R}\le0$.

By [F10], $H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ is a real Hilbert space with the full $W^{1,2}$ inner product; [F2] gives its norm. For any $L_R>0$, [F11] and the pointwise Euclidean inequality $|
abla v\cdot
abla w|\le|
abla v||
abla w|$ give $|a(v,w)|\le(1+L_R)\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}\|w\|_{W^{1,2}}$, so the form is bounded. Also $a(v,v)\ge\min\{1,L_R\}\|v\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, so it is coercive. For $f\in L^2(D_R)$, [F11] gives $\int|fw|\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_2$, and [F12] then gives $|\int fw|\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_2\le\|f\|_2\|w\|_{W^{1,2}}$. Thus [F3] gives a unique zero-Dirichlet weak solution of $(-\Delta+L_R)u=f$. The resolver is linear by uniqueness and positivity preserving: if $f\ge0$, then $-u$ is a weak subsolution of $(-\Delta+L_R)(-u)=-f\le0$ with zero trace, so [F4] gives $u\ge0$.

The lower and upper barriers have the same logarithmic singular part, so $w=u_--u_{s,R}-\psi_R$ extends continuously across every center. Their subsolution and supersolution inequalities imply $\Delta w-c_Rw\ge0$, where $c_R=\kappa\int_0^1\exp((1-t)(u_{s,R}+\psi_R)+tu_-)\,dt\ge0$, extended continuously at the centers. On $\partial D_R$, $w=u_-<0$ (and $w=0$ when $D$ is empty). Applying [F4] to $(-\Delta+c_R)w\le0$ with nonpositive boundary trace gives $w\le0$, hence $v_0=u_--u_{s,R}\le\psi_R$.

Set $G_R(v)=\kappa+L_Rv-\kappa A_Re^v$ and choose $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$. For $v\le\psi_R$, $G_R'(v)=L_R-\kappa A_Re^v\ge0$, so the iteration map $T_R=(-\Delta+L_R)^{-1}G_R$ is order preserving. To prove the lower comparison, put $z=v_0-T_Rv_0$. The logarithmic singularities in $v_0=u_--u_{s,R}$ cancel, so $v_0\in H^1(D_R)$; also $T_Rv_0\in H^1_0(D_R)$. The subsolution inequality of step 1.1 and $\Delta u_{s,R}=4\pi D$ from step 1.2 cancel the Dirac terms and give, distributionally, $\Delta v_0+\kappa(1-e^{u_-})\ge0$. Since $u_-=u_{s,R}+v_0$ and $e^{u_{s,R}}=A_R$, this is $(-\Delta+L_R)v_0\le G_R(v_0)$. The resolvent equation for $T_Rv_0$ therefore makes $z$ a weak subsolution of $(-\Delta+L_R)z\le0$. Its boundary trace is that of $v_0$, namely $u_-|_{\partial D_R}\le0$ because $u_{s,R}=0$ there; the inequality is strict for nonempty $D$ and is equality for the empty divisor. The weak maximum principle [F4], with $L_R>0$, gives $z\le0$, hence $v_0\le T_Rv_0$. For the upper comparison, $\Delta\psi_R=-\kappa$ and the supersolution residual in step 1.2 give $(-\Delta+L_R)\psi_R\ge G_R(\psi_R)$; both $\psi_R$ and $T_R\psi_R$ have zero trace, so positivity of the resolver from step 1.3 gives $T_R\psi_R\le\psi_R$. Thus $v_0\le v_1\le\cdots\le\psi_R$; every iterate after $v_0$ has zero Dirichlet trace. Each has a smooth representative: starting from smooth $v_0$ and $A_R$, rewrite its shifted resolvent equation as a Laplace equation, use boundedness and [F5] for $W^{2,p}$, then [F6]–[F7] and local bootstrapping; this also identifies continuous representatives up to the boundary. These representatives realize the order pointwise.

The monotone iterates have a bounded pointwise limit $v_R$ on the finite disk. If $C\ge\sup_{D_R}(\psi_R-v_0)^2$, then $0\le C-(v_R-v_k)^2\uparrow C$. Applying [F13] and subtracting the finite integral of C gives $\int_{D_R}(v_R-v_k)^2\to0$, so $v_k\to v_R$ in $L^2(D_R)$. For functions $v,w$ with $v_0\le v,w\le\psi_R$, the pointwise mean-value formula gives $|e^v-e^w|\le e^{\psi_R}|v-w|$; hence $\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2\le(L_R+\kappa\|A_R\|_\infty e^{\max\psi_R})\|v-w\|_2$. Subtract the two resolvent equations for $T_Rv,T_Rw$ and test with $u=T_Rv-T_Rw$. The form in step 1.3 satisfies $a(u,u)\ge\min\{1,L_R\}\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, while [F11] and [F12] bound the right side by $\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}$; division when $u\ne0$ (and trivially when $u=0$) gives $\|T_Rv-T_Rw\|_{W^{1,2}}\le\min\{1,L_R\}^{-1}\|G_R(v)-G_R(w)\|_2$. Therefore $T_Rv_k\to T_Rv_R$ in $H^1_0$; the shifted sequence $v_{k+1}=T_Rv_k$ has the same $L^2$ limit as $v_k$, so uniqueness of an $L^2$ limit gives $v_R=T_Rv_R$. It is a weak solution of $-\Delta v_R=\kappa(1-A_Re^{v_R})$ with zero trace.

Since $v_0\le v_R\le\psi_R$ and $A_R$ is bounded on $\overline D_R$, the right-hand side in step 3.1 lies in $L^p(D_R)$ for every finite $p$. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$. The disk is bounded and smooth, so [F5] gives $v_R\in W^{2,p}$; [F6] gives a $C^{1,\beta}$ representative with $\beta>\alpha$ and zero boundary values. The nonlinear right-hand side is then $C^{0,\alpha}$, and [F7] upgrades the weak solution to $C^{2,\alpha}(\overline D_R)$. Repeated local Schauder bootstrapping, using [F9], makes $v_R$ smooth in $D_R$. Setting $u_R=u_{s,R}+v_R$ proves its distributional equation and logarithmic center behavior.

If $u_R$ were positive somewhere, its boundary value is zero and it tends to $-\infty$ at each center, so it would attain a positive interior maximum away from the centers. There $\Delta u_R=\kappa(e^{u_R}-1)>0$ by its equation, contradicting the second-derivative test at a maximum. Thus $u_R\le0$; together with the lower iteration bound in step 2.2 and its limit in step 3.1 this gives $u_-\le u_R\le0$.

Fix a disk $U=B_S(0)$ containing the centers in its interior and let $s=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$. For every sufficiently large $R$, $w_R=u_R-s$ is smooth on $\overline U$. On $\partial U$, steps 1.1 and 5.1 give the uniform bounds $u_--s\le w_R\le-s$, whose endpoints are finite there. On $U$, $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)=\kappa(e^{u_R}-1)\in[-\kappa,0]$. A quadratic barrier $Q(z)=M+\kappa(S^2-|z|^2)/4$, with $M$ larger than the uniform boundary bound, satisfies $\Delta(w_R-Q)\ge0$ and $\Delta(-w_R-Q)\ge0$, and both differences are nonpositive on $\partial U$; the disk maximum principle [F4], with zero lower-order coefficient, yields $|w_R|\le Q$.

On any smaller compact disk $K\Subset U$, [F8] applied on finitely many nested balls and the uniform $L^\infty$ bound of step 6.1 yields uniform $W^{2,p}$ bounds for $w_R$ for every finite $p>2$, since its Laplacian is bounded. For a prescribed $0<\alpha<1$, choose $p>2/(1-\alpha)$ and then $\beta$ with $\alpha<\beta<1-2/p$; [F6] gives a uniform $C^{1,\beta}$ bound on a slightly larger compact disk. As $e^s$ is smooth and $\Delta w_R=\kappa(e^s e^{w_R}-1)$, the right-hand side has a uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bound there; [F9] then yields a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $K$. These bounds are independent of $R$ and are the local compactness estimates used for disk exhaustion.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Let $\kappa>0$ and let $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$ be a finite effective divisor in $\mathbb C$, where the centers $z_j$ are distinct and $m_j\in\mathbb N$; write $N=\sum_jm_j$. For any $a>0$ with $a\ge4N/\kappa$, define
$$u_-(z)=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\log\frac{|z-z_j|^2}{|z-z_j|^2+a}$$
This function is locally integrable and $e^{u_-}$ extends continuously by zero at each center. It satisfies the distributional inequality
$$\left\langle\Delta u_-+\kappa(1-e^{u_-}),\varphi\right\rangle\ge4\pi\sum_jm_j\varphi(z_j)$$
for every nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb C)$, where $\langle\Delta u_-,\varphi\rangle:=\int_{\mathbb C}u_-\Delta\varphi\,dx_1dx_2$. For every $R>\max_j|z_j|$ (with the empty maximum interpreted as $0$), let $D_R=\{|z|<R\}$ and define
$$u_{s,R}(z)=\sum_jm_j\log\frac{R^2|z-z_j|^2}{|R^2-\overline z_jz|^2},\qquad \psi_R(z)=\frac{\kappa}{4}(R^2-|z|^2),\qquad A_R=e^{u_{s,R}}.$$
In the formula for $A_R$, define $A_R$ off the centers and extend it smoothly by zero at each center. Then $u_{s,R}$ vanishes on $\partial D_R$ and $\Delta u_{s,R}=4\pi\sum_jm_j\delta_{z_j}$ in distributions. For every nonnegative $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(D_R)$,
$$\left\langle\Delta(u_{s,R}+\psi_R)+\kappa(1-e^{u_{s,R}+\psi_R}),\varphi\right\rangle\le4\pi\sum_jm_j\varphi(z_j).$$
Also, $u_-\le u_{s,R}+\psi_R$ on $D_R$. Write $H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ for the closure of $C_c^\infty(D_R;\mathbb R)$ in the real Sobolev space $W^{1,2}(D_R;\mathbb R)$. For any constant $L_R\ge\kappa\max_{\overline D_R}(A_Re^{\psi_R})$, define $\mathcal R_R f$ for $f\in L^2(D_R;\mathbb R)$ to be the unique $w\in H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ satisfying
$$\int_{D_R}(\nabla w\cdot\nabla\eta+L_Rw\eta)\,dx_1dx_2=\int_{D_R}f\eta\,dx_1dx_2\qquad(\eta\in H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)).$$
The map $\mathcal R_R:L^2(D_R;\mathbb R)\to H^1_0(D_R;\mathbb R)$ is linear and satisfies $\mathcal R_Rf\ge0$ almost everywhere whenever $f\ge0$ almost everywhere. Define $v_0=u_--u_{s,R}$ away from the centers and extend this difference smoothly across them, where its logarithmic terms cancel. With $G_R(v)=\kappa+L_Rv-\kappa A_Re^v$, one has $G_R(v)\in L^2(D_R;\mathbb R)$ for every real $v\in L^2(D_R;\mathbb R)$ satisfying $v_0\le v\le\psi_R$ almost everywhere, and the iteration is
$$v_{k+1}=\mathcal R_R(G_R(v_k)).$$
It converges pointwise and in $H^1(D_R)$ to a solution $v_R\in C^{2,\alpha}(\overline D_R)$ for every $0<\alpha<1$, with $v_0\le v_R\le\psi_R$ and zero boundary trace. Thus $u_R=u_{s,R}+v_R$ solves the distributional divisor equation, satisfies $u_-\le u_R\le0$, and has $u_R-2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$ smooth at the centers. For the fixed singular function $s(z)=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$, every compact $K\subset\mathbb C$ and every $p>2$ admit constants independent of sufficiently large $R$ such that $u_R-s$ is uniformly bounded in $W^{2,p}(K)$. For each $0<\alpha<1$, choosing $p>2/(1-\alpha)$ also gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}(K)$ bound. These are the local compactness estimates for disk exhaustion.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $1<p<\infty$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, continuous principal coefficients on the closed ball, and $\|b\|_\infty+\|c\|_\infty\le M$. Then every $u\in W^{2,p}(B_R(x_0))$ with $Lu=f\in L^p$ satisfies the scale-invariant estimate
$$\sum_{j=0}^{2}R^{j-2}\max_{|\beta|=j}\|D^\beta u\|_{L^p(B_{R/2}(x_0))}\le C\bigl(R^{-2}\|u\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}+\|f\|_{L^p(B_R(x_0))}\bigr),$$
where $D^0u=u$ and the maximum runs over multi-indices of order $j$,
where $C$ may depend on $n,p,\lambda,\Lambda,R\|b\|_\infty,R^2\|c\|_\infty$ and the modulus of continuity of $A$ on the ball. A radius-independent constant requires uniform control of these dimensionless lower-order bounds and of the modulus. The theorem assumes continuity of $A$; no estimate for merely measurable principal coefficients is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge2$, $0<\alpha<1$, $R>0$, $x_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $L=a^{ij}\partial_i\partial_j+b^i\partial_i+c$ be uniformly elliptic on $B_R(x_0)$ with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, $[A]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\le K$, and $b,c\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$ with finite global Hölder seminorms. Let $u\in C^2(B_R(x_0))\cap L^\infty(B_R(x_0))$ satisfy $Lu=f$ pointwise with $f\in C^{0,\alpha}(B_R(x_0))$. Then $u\in C^{2,\alpha}(B_{R/2}(x_0))$ and
$$\|u\|^{*}_{2,\alpha;B_{R/2}(x_0)}\le C\bigl(\|u\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^2\|f\|_{\infty;B_R(x_0)}+R^{2+\alpha}[f]_{0,\alpha;B_R(x_0)}\bigr),$$
where $C$ depends only on $n,\alpha,\lambda,\Lambda$ and the finite dimensionless coefficient bounds $R^\alpha K+R\|b\|_\infty+R^{1+\alpha}[b]_{0,\alpha}+R^2\|c\|_\infty+R^{2+\alpha}[c]_{0,\alpha}$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $k\ge1$, $1\le p\le\infty$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded $C^k$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]. Then for every open set
$V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ there is a bounded
linear extension operator
$$E:W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K),\qquad (Eu)|_\Omega=u\ \text{a.e. on }\Omega,$$
such that $\operatorname{supp}(Eu)$ is a compact subset of $V$ for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. In particular each bounded $C^k$ domain is a
$W^{k,p}$-extension domain, with an operator whose output is supported in any
prescribed neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$. For $k=0$, extension by zero
is an isometric $L^p$ extension on any open $\Omega$; its output is supported
in the compact set $\overline\Omega\subseteq V$ when $\Omega$ is bounded.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\geq1$. For $Z=\mathbb R$ and for $Z=\mathbb R^n$ with its Euclidean metric:

1. A family $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Z)$ is compact in the uniform topology if and only if it is uniformly closed, equicontinuous, and pointwise bounded.
2. Every pointwise bounded equicontinuous sequence in $C(X,Z)$ has a uniformly convergent subsequence with limit in $C(X,Z)$.

For real-valued families, equicontinuity is uniform over the compact domain, and equicontinuity together with pointwise boundedness gives one bound for all values. The same one-bound conclusion holds for Euclidean-valued families.

Assume Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice through the Poincare and Sobolev suppliers below. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain, and let $L$, $a$ and the real coefficient functions $a^{ij},b^i,c$ be as in [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]], with ellipticity constant $\theta$ and bounds $M_a,M_b,M_c$. Let $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ and $u\in H^1(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ be a real local weak subsolution of $Lu=f$. Suppose the weak sign condition
$$\int_\Omega\bigl(c\,\zeta+b^iD_i\zeta\bigr)dx\ge0\qquad\text{for every }\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\Omega),\ \zeta\ge0,$$
holds, and assume $c\ge0$ a.e. on $\Omega$. Then:

1. **Homogeneous case.** If $f=0$ a.e., then
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^+,$$
with the boundary supremum of [[def-weak-subsolution-and-supersolution-of-a-divergence-form-equation]]. If in addition $b\equiv0$, $c\equiv0$, and $u$ is a weak solution of $Lu=0$, then $\operatorname{ess\,sup}_\Omega u=\sup_{\partial\Omega}u$.

2. **Forcing with signed lower order.** If $b\equiv0$, $c\ge0$ a.e. and $f\in L^q(\Omega)$ for some $q>n/2$ ($q>1$ when $n=2$), then the local inequality extends to all nonnegative $H^1_0(\Omega)$ tests and
$$\operatorname{ess\,sup}_{\Omega}u\le\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^++C\|f^+\|_{L^q(\Omega)},\qquad C=C(n,q,\theta,M_a,M_c,\Omega),$$
where $\Omega$ enters $C$ only through its Poincare constant and volume.

If $u$ is a weak supersolution of $Lu=f$ under either set of hypotheses, apply the corresponding bound to $-u$ for the **same** operator coefficients $(a,b,c)$ and source $-f$. This gives $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^-$ in the homogeneous case and $\operatorname{ess\,inf}_\Omega u\ge-\sup_{\partial\Omega}u^- -C\|f^-\|_{L^q(\Omega)}$ in the forcing case. The maximum-principle conclusions concern real-valued classes and real coefficients.

Assume countable choice for the mean-inequality input. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a domain, and let $u\in C^2(\Omega)$ satisfy $\Delta u\ge0$. If there is $a\in\Omega$ with $u(x)\le u(a)$ for every $x\in\Omega$, then $u$ is constant.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Choose radii $R_k\to\infty$ with every center in $D_{R_k}$. Let $s=2\sum_jm_j\log|z-z_j|$ and $w_k=u_{R_k}-s$. For each compact disk $K$ and each $0<\alpha<1$, [F2] gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on $w_k$ on a slightly larger disk. Thus $(w_k,Dw_k,D^2w_k)$ is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous there. Apply the Euclidean sequence statement [F6] to the finite derivative tuple on each nonempty compact disk. A countable diagonal selection under [A1] then gives locally uniform convergence of $w_k$ and all its derivatives through order two. The fundamental theorem of calculus on coordinate segments identifies the limiting derivative tuple as the first and second derivatives of one $C^2$ function w. Thus the subsequence converges in $C^2$ on every compact disk. Set $h=s+w$.

On every compact set, $e^{u_{R_k}}=e^s e^{w_k}$ converges uniformly to $e^h$. Passing to the limit in the weak divisor equation for $u_{R_k}$ gives $\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi D$ distributionally. Since $s-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ is smooth near each center and $w$ is $C^2$ there, the prescribed logarithmic subtraction extends continuously. The equation for $w$ is $\Delta w=\kappa(e^s e^w-1)$ with smooth coefficient $e^s=|P|^2$; repeated interior Schauder regularity [F4] bootstraps $w$ to $C^\infty$, so each center subtraction is smooth. The bounds $u_-\le u_{R_k}\le0$ pass to the limit, and $u_-(z)\to0$ at infinity; hence $h\le0$ and $h\to0$.

If $h_1,h_2$ are two solutions with the same divisor and boundary condition, $v=h_1-h_2$ extends smoothly across the centers. Subtracting their equations gives $\Delta v-c(z)v=0$, where $c(z)=\kappa\int_0^1 e^{(1-t)h_2+th_1}\,dt\ge0$, extended continuously by $0$ at the centers. On $D_R$, the weak maximum principle [F7] applied to $v$ and $-v$ bounds $|v|$ by $\sup_{\partial D_R}|v|$. This boundary supremum tends to $0$ as $R\to\infty$, so $v=0$ and the scalar solution is unique. When $D$ is empty, $h=0$ is a solution and the same uniqueness argument shows it is the only one.

Suppose $N>0$ and put $w=-h\ge0$. Away from the divisor, $\Delta w=\kappa(1-e^{-w})\le\kappa w$. On $\Omega=(\mathbb R^2\setminus\{z_j\})\times(-\pi/(2\sqrt\kappa),\pi/(2\sqrt\kappa))$, define $U(z,t)=-w(z)\cos(\sqrt\kappa t)$. Then $U\le0$ and $\Delta_{z,t}U=\cos(\sqrt\kappa t)(\kappa w-\Delta w)\ge0$. The finite-punctured plane is path connected (polygonal paths can detour around finitely many points), hence $\Omega$ is connected. The function $w-\varphi$ is nonpositive on $|z|=R_0$ and tends to $0$ at infinity. If it were positive somewhere, its positive maximum would be attained at a finite interior point, where $(\Delta-c)(w-\varphi)<0$, a contradiction. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $e>0$ and $\xi>0$ be real parameters, set $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, identify the oriented Euclidean plane $\mathbb R^2$ with $\mathbb C$ using coordinates $(x_1,x_2)$, and use the Hodge star convention $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$. A field pair is a smooth real one-form $A=A_1dx_1+A_2dx_2$ on the trivial complex line over $\mathbb R^2$ and a smooth function $q:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb C$. Its unit-charge covariant derivative is $D_Aq=dq-iAq$, its curvature is $F_A=dA=B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2$ with $B=\partial_1A_2-\partial_2A_1$, and its transverse energy is
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2.$$
The pair has finite energy when this nonnegative Lebesgue integral is finite. An admissible boundary sector consists of an integer $n$, a radius $R_0$, and smooth functions $\rho>0$ and real $2\pi$-periodic $\phi$ on $r>R_0$ such that $q(r,\theta)=\rho(r,\theta)e^{i(n\theta+\phi(r,\theta))}$ and $\rho\to\sqrt\xi$, $\phi\to0$ uniformly as $r\to\infty$; $n$ is its winding. A gauge transformation is $(q,A)\mapsto(e^{i\chi}q,A+d\chi)$ for a smooth real-valued function $\chi$ on $\mathbb R^2$.

For $n\ge0$, the positive critical first-order equations are $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$; for $n\le0$ the negative equations are $(D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=-e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$. The adjective critical refers to the displayed energy normalization and these square-saturating equations. For a positive-winding solution, its divisor is an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$, where the $z_j\in\mathbb C$ are distinct, the multiplicities $m_j$ are positive integers, $q$ vanishes exactly at the $z_j$, and near each $z_j$ it has the local form $q(z)=(z-z_j)^{m_j}g_j(z)$ with $g_j$ smooth and nonzero there. The degree is $N=\sum_jm_j$; the empty divisor has degree zero. Negative winding uses the conjugate field and reversed orientation, with $N=|n|$.

On the complement of the divisor, define $h=\log(|q|^2/\xi)$. The associated scalar Taubes datum is a real function smooth away from the divisor such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across every $z_j$, $h\to0$ at infinity, and, as a distribution,
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j},\qquad \langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)\quad(\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)).$$
When the limit exists, the magnetic flux is $\Phi(A)=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{|x|<R}B(x)\,dx_1dx_2$. These are mathematical configuration and normalization conventions; they make no assertion that a physical model describes nature.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix $e>0$, $\xi>0$, $\kappa=2e^2\xi$, and an effective finite divisor $D=\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j[z_j]$ on $\mathbb C$ with distinct centers and positive integer multiplicities; let $N=\sum_jm_j$. There is a unique real scalar function $h$, smooth on $\mathbb C\setminus\{z_j\}$, such that $h-2m_j\log|z-z_j|$ extends smoothly across each center, $h\to0$ as $|z|\to\infty$, and
$$\Delta h+\kappa(1-e^h)=4\pi\sum_{j=1}^Jm_j\delta_{z_j}$$
in distributions, where $\langle\delta_z,\psi\rangle=\psi(z)$ for $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$. For $N>0$, $h<0$ off the divisor; for the empty divisor, $h=0$. With $P(z)=\prod_j(z-z_j)^{m_j}$, $s=2\log|P|$, and the orientation $*dx_1=dx_2$, $*dx_2=-dx_1$, the fields
$$q(z)=\sqrt\xi\,e^{(h(z)-s(z))/2}P(z),\qquad A=-\tfrac12 *d(h-s)$$
extend smoothly across the centers and solve $(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q=0$ and $B=e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$, where $D_A=d-iA$ and $B\,dx_1\wedge dx_2=dA$. They have finite energy
$$E(A,q)=\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+|D_{A,1}q|^2+|D_{A,2}q|^2+\frac{e^2}{2}(|q|^2-\xi)^2\right)dx_1dx_2$$
and flux $\int_{\mathbb R^2}B\,dx_1dx_2=2\pi N$. For every $0<\alpha<\sqrt\kappa$ and every multi-index $\beta$, $|\partial^\beta h(z)|=O(e^{-\alpha|z|})$ as $|z|\to\infty$; the curvature $B$ and covariant gradient $D_Aq$ have the same exponential decay. On the exterior of a disk, the local gauge $e^{-i\arg P}$ gives $q_{\mathrm{ext}}=\sqrt\xi e^{h/2}$ and $A_{\mathrm{ext}}=-\tfrac12 *dh$, so the fields approach the vacuum exponentially in that exterior gauge; the raw global representative $q$ need not have an exponentially small phase correction. Negative winding $-N$ is obtained by complex conjugation and $A\mapsto-A$, with flux $-2\pi N$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $M$ be an oriented smooth $n$-manifold with boundary, $n\geq1$, and let $\eta\in\Omega_c^{n-1}(M)$. With $j:\partial M\hookrightarrow M$ and the outward-normal-first orientation,
$$\int_M d\eta=\int_{\partial M}j^*\eta.$$
An empty boundary contributes zero; in dimension one its integral is a finite signed sum of point values.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n \ge 1$,
let $S^{n-1} \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be the unit sphere, and let $\sigma$ be the
set function of [[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]. Then $\sigma$
is a finite Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$, and for every Borel measurable
$f : \mathbb R^n \to [0,\infty]$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R^n} f(x)\,d\lambda_n(x) = \int_0^\infty \int_{S^{n-1}} f(r\omega) r^{n-1}\,d\sigma(\omega)\,dr.$$
Moreover, $\sigma$ is the unique Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ with this
property.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix $n \ge 1$
and write
$$S^{n-1}:=\{\omega \in \mathbb R^n : |\omega|=1\}.$$
Let
$$\Phi:\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}\longrightarrow(0,\infty)\times S^{n-1},\qquad \Phi(x)=(|x|,x/|x|).$$
This map is continuous. If $E\subseteq S^{n-1}$ is Borel, then
$(0,1]\times E$ is Borel and
$$\{r\omega:\omega\in E,\ 0<r\le1\}=\Phi^{-1}((0,1]\times E)$$
is Borel in $\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ by
[[thm-continuous-preimages-of-borel-sets-are-borel]], hence Borel in
$\mathbb R^n$ by [[thm-borel-sigma-algebra-of-a-subspace-is-the-trace]]. It is
therefore Lebesgue measurable by [[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]].
Define
$$\sigma(E):=n\,\lambda_n(\{r\omega : \omega \in E,\ 0<r\le 1\}).$$

The next theorem proves that this is a Borel measure on $S^{n-1}$ and that it
is exactly the surface measure needed for polar coordinates.

Define the real current one-form $j=j_1dx_1+j_2dx_2$ by $j_i=\operatorname{Im}(\overline qD_{A,i}q)$. Expanding the squares and using $[D_{A,1},D_{A,2}]q=-iBq$ gives
$$|D_Aq|^2=|(D_{A,1}+iD_{A,2})q|^2+\partial_1j_2-\partial_2j_1+B|q|^2.$$
Also, direct expansion gives
$$\frac{B^2}{2e^2}+\frac{e^2}{2}(\xi-|q|^2)^2=\frac{(B-e^2(\xi-|q|^2))^2}{2e^2}+B(\xi-|q|^2).$$
Adding these identities yields the positive-winding disk identity with boundary term $\int_{D_R}(\partial_1j_2-\partial_2j_1)$. Repeating the expansion with $D_{A,1}-iD_{A,2}$ and $B+e^2(\xi-|q|^2)$ gives the negative-winding identity with the opposite signs.

Enlarge the exterior radius in [F1] if necessary so $R_0\ge1$. For $r>R_0$, let $Q(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}(|q|^2-\xi)^2ds$ and $K(r)=\int_{\partial D_r}|D_{A,\tau}q|^2ds$, where $D_{A,\tau}$ is the covariant derivative in the unit tangent direction and $ds=r\,d\theta=r\,d\sigma$ by [F7]. The polar formula [F7] and Fubini [F4] identify $\int_{R_0}^\infty Q(r)\,dr$ with $\int_{|x|>R_0}(|q|^2-\xi)^2dx$ and $\int_{R_0}^\infty K(r)\,dr$ with the integral of $|D_{A,\tau}q|^2$ there, which is bounded by the finite kinetic energy. In particular $Q,K\in L^1([R_0,\infty))$ and are measurable. For each integer $m\ge1$, the set $S_m=\{r\ge R_0:Q(r)>1/m\}$ has finite measure. Its complement has divergent $\int dr/r$, since removing a finite-measure set from a half-line cannot make the logarithmic integral finite. If $rK(r)\ge1/m$ for every sufficiently large $r\notin S_m$, then $\int K(r)dr\ge m^{-1}\int_{[R,\infty)\setminus S_m}dr/r=\infty$, contradiction. Thus there is an unbounded set of radii with $Q(r)\le1/m$ and $rK(r)<1/m$. By [A1] select an increasing sequence $r_m\to\infty$ from these sets. Along it, [F6, F7] give $\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\le2\pi\xi r_m+\sqrt{2\pi r_mQ(r_m)}=O(r_m)$, and
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}j\right|\le\left(\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}|q|^2ds\right)^{1/2}K(r_m)^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$

Uniform convergence $|q|\to\sqrt\xi$ gives $|q|^2\ge\xi/2$ for sufficiently large $r$. On $\partial D_r$, $j=|q|^2(d(n\theta+\phi)-A)$, so $\int_{\partial D_r}A=2\pi n-\int_{\partial D_r}j/|q|^2$ because $\phi$ is single-valued and periodic. Also $|j_\tau|=|\operatorname{Im}(\overline qD_{A,\tau}q)|\le|q||D_{A,\tau}q|$, hence $|j_\tau|/|q|^2\le\sqrt{2/\xi}|D_{A,\tau}q|$. Along the sequence from step 1.2, Cauchy--Schwarz and [F7] give
$$\left|\int_{\partial D_{r_m}}\frac{j}{|q|^2}\right|\le\sqrt{\frac{2}{\xi}}(2\pi r_mK(r_m))^{1/2}\longrightarrow0.$$
By [F3], $\int_{D_{r_m}}B\to2\pi n$.

Integrate the positive-winding disk identity from step 1.1 over $D_{r_m}$ and use [F3] on the current term. The two square integrals are nonnegative, while the boundary-current integral tends to zero by step 1.2 and the flux integral tends to $2\pi n$ by step 2.1. By [F5], the integrals of the nonnegative energy and square densities over the increasing disks converge to their plane integrals, so taking the limit gives the positive-sign exact identity and hence $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi n$ for $n\ge0$. For $n\le0$, apply the positive-sign identity from step 1.1 to $(\overline q,-A)$, whose winding is $-n\ge0$; its energy is unchanged and its curvature changes sign. The resulting identity is exactly the negative-sign identity for $(A,q)$ and gives $E(A,q)\ge-2\pi\xi n$. Thus the bound is $E(A,q)\ge2\pi\xi|n|$, and both identities hold when $n=0$ as well.

For each fixed divisor, [F2] supplies a smooth pair satisfying the relevant first-order equations. Its square terms in step 1.1 vanish identically; the sequence estimates of steps 1.2–2.1 apply because [F2] gives finite energy and the same boundary sector. Hence its energy is exactly $2\pi\xi|n|$. The lower bound of step 3.1 applies to every admissible same-winding configuration, so this pair is an absolute transverse energy minimum, without radial or unit-winding assumptions.

Let $(a,\eta)$ be a smooth compactly supported variation of a minimizing pair, and set $A_t=A+ta$, $q_t=q+t\eta$; for any field expression $F$, define $\delta F:=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\right|_{t=0}F(A_t,q_t)$. For sufficiently small $t$, the fields remain in the same boundary sector; outside the compact support they equal the original fields. Thus the boundary-current limit in the disk identity is unchanged and the flux is unchanged by Stokes applied to $d a$. The energy along this variation is the constant $2\pi\xi|n|$ plus the squared $L^2$ norms of the two first-order residuals in step 1.1. Both residuals vanish at $t=0$; differentiating the squared norms gives $E'(0)=0$ and
$$E''(0)=2\int_{\mathbb R^2}\left(|\delta(D_{A,1}\pm iD_{A,2})q|^2+\frac{|\delta(B\mp e^2(\xi-|q|^2))|^2}{2e^2}\right)dx_1dx_2\ge0,$$
with the upper signs for $n\ge0$ and lower signs for $n\le0$ (either choice when $n=0$). Therefore the first variation vanishes and no smooth compactly supported same-sector perturbation lowers the energy. Distinct divisors give distinct possible minimizing fields, so no cross-divisor uniqueness follows.
